does: Cuts food into fine, even strips the length of a matchstick.

intro.what: Julienne cuts vegetables into fine, even strips.
intro.why: It teaches you to build a precise cut from flat sheets and keep the strips consistent.

how: Cut the vegetable into lengths as long as the strips you want.
Slice each length into thin, flat sheets.
Stack a few sheets and slice them lengthwise into strips as wide as the sheets are thick.
For a leek, split a length open, lay the layers flat and slice along the grain.

cues.text: Fine strips of one length that bend without snapping and fall apart from each other.

mistakes.mistake: Stacking too many sheets, so the pile slides and the strips come out as wedges.
mistakes.fix: Stack only a few sheets at a time and keep the pile flat.

quiz.question: Which shape is the aim of julienne?
quiz.because: Julienne means fine strips of an even length and width, rather than cubes or wedges.

quiz.question: How do the flat sheets become strips?
choices: Slice the stack across its width into short pieces.
Cut across them into cubes immediately.
quiz.because: Slicing lengthwise keeps the intended strip length. Match the width of each strip to the thickness of the sheets.

quiz.question: Which pile most closely matches julienne?
choices: Fine strips of a similar length that fall apart from each other.
A wet mash of tiny pieces.
quiz.because: Fine, even strips that separate from each other show a consistent julienne cut.

quiz.question: The stack slides and your strips become wedges. What would you change?
choices: Stack more sheets to make it heavier.
Use fewer sheets and keep the pile flat.
Press the loose pile into a tall heap.
quiz.because: A tall stack can slide and turn the cuts into wedges. Keep the stack small and flat.

comes_after.why: A julienne starts as thin, even slices.
